heroHeadline: FIFA Crisis Turns Legal: UEFA Preps Criminal Complaint Against Infantino as Italy Withdraws Support
heroSubtitle: A month after Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time to win the World Cup Final at MetLife Stadium (July 19), the tournament's aftermath has escalated from a governance dispute into formal legal jeopardy for FIFA president Gianni Infantino. Italy's football federation (FIGC) withdrew support for his re-election bid (Aug 26), citing his handling of the abandoned World Cup stake-sale plan and joining England, Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland, New Zealand, Scotland, Israel, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and all six Nordic federations. The next day, court filings in Manhattan and southern Florida revealed UEFA is preparing a criminal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code for 'criminal mismanagement,' seeking discovery from two Florida-based FIFA entities over the abandoned plan's $4.2 billion valuation, which UEFA's lawyers called 'fraudulently off-market' (Aug 27). It follows a widening federation revolt through August — FIFA fired COO Kevin Lamour (Aug 17) after he accused Infantino of misleading staff; Infantino defied a CONCACAF request and attended a Caribbean Football Union event in the Dominican Republic (Aug 22); all six Nordic federations declared 'lost confidence' in him (Aug 23); and UEFA president Aleksander Čeferin said Infantino must either step down or 'have a candidate against him' at the March 18, 2027 election in Rabat (Aug 24).
